The willow flute is a northern European folk aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.221.11, an overtone flute. It is a simple tube with no fingerholes, with a grooved plug inserted at one end and a side-blown edge cut beside it. The player changes the force of the breath and covers or opens the end of the tube with a finger to get different fundamentals and overtone series, and cannot play equal temperament. It was originally made from green willow bark in spring and is now usually plastic tube. Nordic groups use it in traditional line-ups; Karelian folk ensembles also use the birch-bark variant. The related kalyuka is a Russian and Ukrainian overtone flute without holes, blown after the summer hay harvest together with percussion.
柳木長笛為無指孔泛音笛，音色由基音與其泛音列構成，不能奏出十二平均律音階。吹奏者: The willow flute is an overtone flute with no fingerholes; its notes come from a fundamental and its overtone series, and it cannot play a twelve-tone equal-tempered scale. The player controls volume and pitch by the force of the air blown at the edge, and covers or opens the tube end with a finger to get two sets of fundamentals and overtones. Compared with the related kalyuka, another overtone flute without fingerholes, the kalyuka partly closes the top opening with the tongue and changes notes by opening and closing side holes or the tube end, reaching the high notes by overblowing.
柳木长笛属北欧民间泛音长笛，无指孔，靠气息与管端开合取得泛音；原始以春季绿柳皮制: The willow flute is a Nordic folk overtone flute with no fingerholes, taking its overtones from the breath and from opening and closing the end of the tube; it was originally made from green willow bark in spring, which loses its sound once dry, and is now plastic. Similar instruments appear in Polish folk poetry, made by a different method; the Karelian variant uses birch bark. The kalyuka tradition of Russia and Ukraine makes the instrument from hollow plant stems after the summer harvest and plays it with percussion, and it was discovered in 1980 by students of the Moscow and St Petersburg conservatoires. Today it is used by the Swedish group Hedningarna, by Anders Norudde and by Nordic groups.
